name: Negotiation Skills
objectives: Given a real pay or price negotiation, write a one-page plan with your goal, walk-away point, plan B and the other side's needs, with every part filled in before you talk

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Preparing: your goal, your walk-away point and their needs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page negotiation plan before you talk.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real pay or price negotiation, you will write a one-page plan with your goal, walk-away point, plan B and the other side's needs, with every part filled in before you talk.
Most of a negotiation is won before it starts. Preparing means answering three questions on paper.
Your goal: what would a great but realistic result be? Be specific: "$19 an hour and Saturdays off" or "$4.50 a case, delivered weekly". Your walk-away point: the worst deal you would still accept. Below it, you say no. Know your plan B, the best thing you can do if there is no deal, such as another job offer, another supplier or keeping your current job. A strong plan B gives you confidence.
The other side's needs: what do they want, and what are they worried about? An employer may need someone reliable who can start soon. A sponsor may want your posts to reach their customers. A supplier may want a steady monthly order. When you know their needs, you can offer things that cost you little but matter to them.
Step by step:
- Write your goal, with numbers.
- Write your walk-away point.
- Write your plan B if there is no deal.
- List the other side's needs and worries.
- List things you could offer that matter to them.
Words to know:
- Walk-away point: the worst deal you would still accept; below it you say no.
- Plan B: what you will do if there is no deal. Negotiation books call it a BATNA.
- Negotiation: talking with someone to reach an agreement you both accept.
Try it now: Pick a real negotiation coming up: a pay talk, a price with a supplier or customer, rent, or a sponsorship. Write your goal, walk-away point, plan B and the other side's top two needs.
You can now prepare for a negotiation by writing your goal, walk-away point, plan B and the other side's needs.

options: The best thing you can do if there is no deal
A second copy of your plan
check.why: Your plan B is your best option if there is no deal, such as another offer or keeping your current job.

check.q: You are preparing to ask a supplier for a better price. What do you write down about them?
options: Nothing; only your own goal matters
What they want and worry about, such as a steady monthly order
check.why: Knowing the other side's needs helps you offer things that cost you little but matter to them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Asking with confidence
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a clear opening ask with a reason, then stop talking.
This lesson builds toward: When you open a negotiation, you will make a clear ask a little above your goal with a reason, then stop talking, in one or two sentences.
Many people never get more because they never ask. The first number said out loud often shapes the whole talk, so it helps to make a clear, reasonable ask yourself. Aim a little above your goal so there is room to move, but keep it something you can explain.
Give a reason: "Based on the pay for this job in our area and my two years running a kitchen line, I am asking for $21 an hour." Or for a business: "For a 12-month order paid on time, we are asking for $4.20 a case." Then stop talking. The silence can feel awkward, but it gives them time to think. Do not argue against yourself.
Ask questions too, and listen to the answers: "What is most important to you in this deal?" "What flexibility do you have on the start date?" The answers tell you what you can trade.
Step by step:
- Choose an opening ask a little above your goal.
- Write one reason you can explain.
- Say the ask and the reason calmly.
- Stop talking and wait.
- Ask open questions and listen for what they need.
Words to know:
- Opening ask: the first thing you ask for in a negotiation.
- Anchor: the first number said; it often shapes the rest of the talk.
Try it now: Write your opening ask and one reason for your real negotiation. Say it out loud three times in a calm voice, and stop for five full seconds after each time.
You can now make a clear opening ask with a reason, stay silent, and ask questions that reveal the other side's needs.

check.q: Why is it helpful to make the first reasonable number yourself?
options: The first number said out loud often shapes the whole talk
The other side must accept it
It shows you do not care
check.why: The lesson says the first number often shapes the talk, so a clear ask with a reason helps you.

check.q: You just made your ask with a reason, and the room goes quiet. What do you do?
options: Explain again why you might not deserve it
Stay quiet and let them think
check.why: Silence gives them time to think; talking can lead you to argue against yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Trading instead of giving in
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use "if... then..." trades so you never give something for nothing.
This lesson builds toward: When the other side pushes back on your number, you will offer an "If you can..., then I can..." trade instead of giving in, naming at least two things besides money that you could trade.
When the other side pushes back, do not just drop your number. Trade. Every time you give something, ask for something back. The simple tool is "If you can..., then I can...".
Look for things that are cheap for one side and valuable to the other. A worker: "If you can't move on the hourly rate, could we review it after 90 days, or add one extra paid day off?" A small business: "If you pay upfront, then I can take 5 percent off." An athlete with a sponsor: "If you want two extra posts, then I would need a higher fee or free product for the team."
Pay is not the only thing on the table. Think about start date, schedule, training, equipment, delivery, payment terms, length of contract, and title. More things to trade means more ways to a deal both sides like.
Step by step:
- Never give something for nothing.
- Use "If you can..., then I can...".
- List what is cheap for you but valuable to them.
- Look beyond money: schedule, start date, training, delivery, terms.
- Check every trade against your walk-away point.
Words to know:
- Trade: giving something only when you get something back.
- Concession: something you give up during a negotiation.
- Terms: the details of a deal, such as when and how payment happens.
Try it now: For your real negotiation, list three things you could offer and three things you could ask for besides money. Write two "If you can..., then I can..." sentences.
You can now trade concessions with "if... then..." instead of giving things away.

check.q: What does trading mean in a negotiation?
options: Giving in to end the talk
Asking for something back each time you give something
check.why: Trading means every time you give something, you ask for something back.

check.q: An employer cannot raise the hourly rate. What is a good trade to ask for?
options: Ask them to promise a raise someday
A pay review after 90 days or an extra paid day off
check.why: Things besides money, like a 90-day review or a day off, can make the deal work for both sides.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Staying calm under pressure
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize pressure tactics and respond calmly.
This lesson builds toward: When someone uses a pressure tactic, you will respond calmly by asking for time, or say no politely to an offer below your walk-away point, without agreeing on the spot.
Some people use pressure to rush you: "This offer ends today," "Take it or leave it," a very low first offer, long silences, or one person acting tough while another acts friendly. These tactics work by making you feel you must decide now.
Your best tool is time. It is almost always fine to say: "Thank you. I'd like to take until tomorrow to think it over." Slow your breathing, keep your voice level and look at your written plan. If the offer is below your walk-away point, you can say no politely: "I appreciate it, but I can't make that work."
Stay respectful even if they do not. Talk about the problem, not the person. Being calm and polite keeps the door open for a better offer later. If anyone threatens you or asks you to do something dishonest or unsafe, walk away.
Step by step:
- Notice the pressure: deadlines, take-it-or-leave-it, very low offers.
- Breathe and slow down.
- Look at your plan and walk-away point.
- Ask for time: "I'd like until tomorrow to think it over."
- Say no politely if it is below your walk-away point.
Words to know:
- Pressure tactic: a trick to rush you into deciding before you are ready.
- Lowball offer: an offer far below what is fair.
Try it now: Write your calm reply to three pressure lines: "This offer ends today," "Take it or leave it," and a lowball offer. Say each reply out loud in a level voice.
You can now spot pressure tactics and respond calmly by asking for time or saying no politely.

options: "Let me send you the details by email."
check.why: Deadlines like "ends today" try to rush you into deciding now.

check.q: The other side gets rude during the talk. What should you do?
options: Agree to anything to end it
Stay respectful and talk about the problem, not the person
check.why: Staying calm and polite keeps the door open for a better offer later.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting it in writing
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Confirm an agreement in writing and read it before you sign.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of any deal, you will confirm every agreed point in writing and read it before you sign, with price, dates and terms listed the same day.
A deal you only said out loud is easy to forget or remember differently. At the end of any negotiation, sum it up out loud: "So we agreed $20 an hour, starting 3 November, with a pay review after 90 days." Then put it in writing.
For a job, ask for a written offer letter. For a business deal, send a short email the same day that lists every point you agreed: price, amounts, dates, payment terms and who does what. Ask them to reply to confirm.
Read every page before you sign, and make sure it matches what was agreed. Do not sign anything blank or that you do not understand. For big or long contracts, such as NIL or sponsorship deals, leases, loans or business partnerships, have a lawyer, a trusted agent, a legal aid clinic or your school's compliance office review it first. An AI assistant can explain hard words in a contract, but it is not a lawyer, and do not paste in private details such as ID or bank numbers.
Step by step:
- Sum up the deal out loud.
- Ask for a written offer or send a summary email the same day.
- List price, amounts, dates, terms and who does what.
- Ask them to reply to confirm.
- Read every page before you sign; get big contracts reviewed.
Words to know:
- Offer letter: a written job offer that states pay, start date and other terms.
- Contract: a written agreement that the law can enforce.
Try it now: Write a short summary email for a deal (real or practice) that lists price or pay, dates, terms and who does what, and ends with: "Please reply to confirm this matches your understanding."
You can now sum up a deal, confirm it in writing and know when to get a contract reviewed.

check.q: What is the best written proof of a new job deal?
check.why: For a job, the lesson says to ask for a written offer letter.

check.q: You are handed a contract with a blank section to "fill in later". What do you do?
options: Sign quickly so you do not lose the deal
Ask an AI to sign it for you
Do not sign until it is complete and you understand it
check.why: Never sign anything blank or that you do not understand.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Negotiating pay and price
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Research a fair number and negotiate a job offer or a price.
This lesson builds toward: Before a pay or price talk, you will research a fair number using pay data, job postings or three quotes, and your own costs, using at least one trusted source. When the other side pushes back on your number, you will offer an "If you can..., then I can..." trade instead of giving in, naming at least two things besides money that you could trade.
Pay: research before you talk. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook (bls.gov/ooh) lists typical pay for hundreds of jobs. Job postings show ranges too. In California, employers with 15 or more employees must put the pay scale in job postings, and an applicant can ask for the pay scale of the job they applied for. California employers also generally may not ask about your past pay, but they may ask what pay you expect. Rules differ by state, so check your state labor department.
When you get an offer: thank them, show you are excited, and ask for time if you need it. Then counter with a reason: "I'm excited about this role. Based on the posted range and my forklift certification, could you do $22?" If pay can't move, trade: start date, schedule, training or a review after 90 days.
Price: for buying, get at least three quotes so you know the going rate. For selling, know your costs so you never agree below what keeps your business alive. Offer options instead of discounts: a smaller package for less, or a lower price for a bigger order or faster payment.
Step by step:
- Research the going rate: bls.gov/ooh, job postings or three quotes.
- Set your goal and walk-away point from that research.
- Thank them and show interest.
- Counter with a number and a reason.
- If money can't move, trade other terms.
- Confirm the final deal in writing.
Words to know:
- Pay scale: the salary or hourly range an employer expects to pay for a job.
- Counteroffer: your answer to an offer, asking for different terms.
- Quote: a price someone offers for a job or product.
Official sources:
- California Labor Commissioner: Equal Pay Act FAQ (pay scales, salary history)
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page plan for a real pay or price negotiation using real research. Role-play it with a friend who uses one pressure tactic, then write the follow-up email that confirms the deal.
You can now research a fair number, counter a job offer or price with a reason, and close the deal in writing.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Plan on paper The plan is missing the goal, walk-away point, plan B or the other side's needs. All four parts are written, specific and realistic. The other side's needs are linked to things you could offer them. Fair number researched The goal is a guess with no source. The goal is based on at least one trusted source, such as pay data, job postings or three quotes. Names the source and, for selling, shows the price covers your costs. Clear ask No number, or a number with no reason. A clear opening ask a little above the goal, with a reason, and then silence. The ask also includes a question to learn what matters to the other side. Trades, not give-ins Dropped the number when pushed, with nothing in return. Used at least one "If you can..., then I can..." trade in the role-play. Offered two or more trades besides money that cost little but matter to the other side. Calm under pressure Agreed on the spot or got upset when pushed. Asked for time or said no politely, and stayed respectful. Named the pressure tactic afterward and how they handled it. Deal in writing No follow-up email, or it leaves out agreed points. The email lists every agreed point (price or pay, dates, terms) and asks them to confirm. The email is short, polite and ready to send the same day. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where can US workers look up typical pay for many jobs?
options: The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh
check.why: The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists typical pay for hundreds of jobs.

check.q: A customer asks you for a discount. What is a good option to offer?
options: A lower price for a bigger order or faster payment
Half price with nothing in return
check.why: Offering options instead of plain discounts protects your costs while helping the customer.
